newsitem.title: FRANCE: French teachers, other unions in Oct 17 strike call.
newsitem.headline: French teachers, other unions in Oct 17 strike call.

text.p: France's main teachers unions on Wednesday joined other labour groups in calling for a nationwide strike on October 17 to protest at government austerity plans.

The five biggest teachers unions, which held a one-day strike last month over government plans to eliminate 2,300 jobs in education next year, also demanded a meeting with Prime Minister Alain Juppe to debate the proposed staff cuts.
The unions, which represent about 825,000 teachers, said they had the backing of 70 percent of the French people.

In a related action, the railways section of the Communist-led CGT trades union gave notice of its intention to take part in next week's stoppages and urged its members to stay away from work from 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) on October 16 to 6 p.m. (1600 GMT) on October 18.

The major civil service unions and unions at the French gas and electricity utilities GDF and EDF have previously announced they too will take part, along with rail workers belonging to the more moderate Force Ouvriere and CFDT unions.

Juppe's popularity is at an all-time low and his government is under fire from voters and parliamentarians alike for its austere budget and economic policies. The unemployment rate reached a record 12.6 percent in August.
The spending and job cuts are intended to help France qualify to take part in a planned single European Union currency from 1999.

Unions have been predicting significant unrest in coming months, but President Jacques Chirac told the cabinet on Wednesday that economic, defence and education reforms were on track and he urged ministers to stay the course.

"The current always runs strongest when you get to the middle of the river. We cannot turn around because that would be a step backwards," Chirac told a cabinet meeting, according to government spokesman Alain Lamassoure.

The CGT said it was joining the strike because both the government and management of the SNCF national railway authority were slow in putting in place agreements concluded after a wave of public transport strikes late last year which virtually paralysed France for more than three weeks.
It blamed management for "reactivating its job reduction policy, reorganisations...and for openly publicising its wish to consider suspending the accords obtained in 1995".
